description: GeoFarmer is a team aimed at utilising Geospatial knowledge to building a simple but robust mobile app for farmers to take decisions. The farmers shoild be able to select suitable plots for suitable crops with respect to current weather and soil conditions. Preferable teammates should have some level of geospatial knowledge.
summary:
GeoFarmervis a mobile-friendly geospatial agricultural decision-support application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, under the theme “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data.” The project focuses on helping smallholder farmers in Ejura-Sekyedumase Municipality, Ghana, make informed crop selection and rotation decisions to improve soil health and adapt to changing climatic conditions.

The application integrates NASA SRTM elevation data, ISRIC SoilGrids datasets and farm records to assess 237 digitised farm parcels. Using GIS, Python, machine learning and artificial intelligence, GeoFarmer evaluates soil and terrain characteristics, ranks crop suitability and provides parcel-specific crop rotation recommendations.

Its features include interactive farm mapping, soil and environmental assessment, K-means clustering for identifying similar land zones, AI-powered agricultural assistance and farm history management. The system also learns from recorded farming outcomes to improve future recommendations.

Developed with ArcGIS Pro, Python, PostgreSQL/PostGIS, Next.js, React and MapLibre GL, GeoFarmer transforms geospatial information into accessible agricultural insights.

Ultimately, the project seeks to promote sustainable soil management, informed crop rotation and climate-resilient agriculture while supporting farmers and agricultural extension officers in making evidence-based decisions.
details:
GeoFarmer is a mobile-friendly web application designed to help smallholder farmers in Ejura-Sekyedumase Municipality, Ashanti Region, Ghana, make informed decisions about what to plant in the next farming season. The project focuses on improving crop rotation practices, maintaining soil health and supporting agricultural adaptation to changing climatic conditions. It was developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the theme "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data".

GeoFarmer integrates NASA SRTM elevation data, ISRIC SoilGrids datasets and farm records to generate transparent crop suitability scores, crop rotation recommendations and easy-to-understand explanations. The application is designed to support farmers' knowledge and judgement rather than replace their decision-making.

The application begins with an interactive map containing 237 digitised farm parcels created in ArcGIS Pro. Users can explore different map layers representing crops, land zones, soil levels, sand content, slope and elevation. These layers provide a spatial understanding of the agricultural landscape and the characteristics of individual farms.

For each farm parcel, GeoFarmer extracts and processes environmental information from NASA SRTM elevation data at 30-metre resolution and SoilGrids soil datasets at 250-metre resolution. The extracted information includes elevation, slope, sand content, soil moisture classes, and relative levels of soil pH, organic carbon and nitrogen. These environmental characteristics provide the foundation for assessing the suitability of different crops across the study area.

GeoFarmer uses a transparent rule-based scoring engine to compare the environmental conditions of each parcel with the requirements of different crops. The assessment considers six factors: temperature, soil pH, rainfall, soil texture, slope and nitrogen. Each crop receives a suitability score, and the application explains the contribution of individual factors to the final result. Where information is unavailable, the system does not invent or estimate values. Instead, it identifies missing information and indicates how many factors were available when generating a particular score.

The application also provides crop rotation recommendations based on the historical planting records of individual parcels. It discourages farmers from repeatedly planting the same crop or crops belonging to the same family. It prioritises legumes after cereals because legumes can contribute to soil nitrogen restoration. It also gives preference to legumes in parcels with relatively low soil nitrogen or organic carbon levels. Each recommendation is accompanied by an explanation and alternative crop options.

To improve its recommendations over time, GeoFarmer incorporates machine learning through k-means clustering. This technique groups farm parcels into land zones based on similarities in their terrain and soil characteristics. It also identifies parcels with similar environmental conditions. When farmers record their seasonal farming outcomes as poor, fair or good, the system adjusts the suitability scores for the corresponding crop on that parcel and its environmentally similar neighbouring parcels.

Artificial intelligence is integrated into the application to make technical information easier for farmers to understand. An AI model generates short, plain-language summaries for individual farm parcels and powers a chat assistant accessible throughout the application. The AI is restricted to information available within GeoFarmer and cannot independently introduce unsupported facts. An automatic verification mechanism checks that recommended crops agree with the rule-based results, numerical values exist in the underlying data and no unknown crops or unrealistic promises are introduced. If verification fails, the application falls back to a rules-based response. Farmers can also describe their planting activities in their own words, allowing the AI to populate the relevant data-entry fields for their confirmation.

GeoFarmer maintains the integrity of farming records through a season-based record management system. Every new planting creates a separate seasonal record rather than replacing an earlier one. Corrections are also logged, ensuring that historical farming information remains available for future analysis.

The project provides several benefits for agricultural decision-making. First, it promotes better crop rotation by discouraging continuous planting of the same crop family and encouraging practices that can help restore soil nitrogen. Second, it incorporates soil health into crop recommendations by prioritising legumes where nitrogen and organic carbon levels are relatively low. Third, it promotes transparency by classifying information as Observed, Relative, Not available or Simulated. This helps users distinguish measured information from relative indicators and demonstration data. Fourth, its mobile-friendly design, plain-language explanations and natural-language data entry make it accessible to farmers using smartphones. Finally, the application can improve over time as farmers record their seasonal outcomes, providing additional information for refining future recommendations.

The intended impact of GeoFarmer is to support smallholder farmers and agricultural extension officers in making more informed and resilient crop rotation decisions, particularly as rainfall patterns become increasingly unpredictable. For farmers, the application aims to reduce soil depletion, minimise crop failure risks and encourage more efficient use of limited water and fertiliser resources. For extension officers, it provides a shared and explainable spatial view of agricultural parcels that can support advisory services and seasonal follow-ups. At the regional level, GeoFarmer demonstrates how NASA Earth observation data and geospatial technologies can be transformed into practical agricultural decision-support information for local communities. The application remains a decision-support tool, with farmers and agricultural experts retaining responsibility for final planting decisions.

The development of GeoFarmer involved several technologies and software tools. ArcGIS Pro was used to digitise the 237 farm parcels, derive slope from the elevation model and perform zonal statistics for individual parcels. NASA SRTM 30-metre elevation data provided the terrain information used to calculate elevation and slope and to support the application's map visualisations. ISRIC SoilGrids supplied soil information, including sand content and relative soil pH, organic carbon and nitrogen levels.

Python was used for geospatial data processing, with libraries including GeoPandas, Rasterio, rasterstats, Pandas and NumPy. These tools supported the extraction of information from the geodatabase, correction of duplicate identifiers, resolution of mixed measurement units, identification of missing values and generation of a data-quality report.

PostgreSQL with PostGIS was used as the database management system. It stores farm parcels as spatial geometries alongside farmer records, crop histories, environmental attributes and information about data sources. The web application was developed using Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. These technologies support the mobile-first interface, including the farm map, parcel information, crop suitability assessments, rotation recommendations and farm management pages. MapLibre GL was used to develop the interactive map and enable users to switch between different spatial data layers.

Machine learning was implemented using k-means clustering in TypeScript to identify land zones, determine similar parcels and incorporate seasonal farming outcomes into future recommendations. A large language model powers the AI features, including plain-language summaries, the chat assistant and natural-language data entry. Development and GIS processing were carried out using laptops, while smartphones and web browsers were used to test the application's accessibility and functionality.

One of the most innovative aspects of GeoFarmer is its combination of explainable agricultural rules, machine learning and artificial intelligence within a single geospatial decision-support platform. Rather than allowing AI to generate unrestricted agricultural recommendations, the application uses its existing data and rule-based results as the foundation for AI-generated explanations. Its automatic fact-checking mechanism helps prevent unsupported numerical claims, incorrect crop recommendations and unrealistic promises. Missing information is clearly identified instead of being replaced with fabricated values.

Another innovative feature is the integration of environmental similarities and actual seasonal farming outcomes. By grouping parcels according to their terrain and soil characteristics, GeoFarmer can use information from similar farms to improve future recommendations. This creates an opportunity for the application to become more responsive to local agricultural conditions as additional farming records are collected.

The application also introduces a data transparency system in which every environmental value is classified as Observed, Relative, Not available or Simulated. This is particularly important when working with soil maps that provide relative information rather than direct field measurements. The system presents such information as low, medium or high indicators instead of treating them as exact measured values. Furthermore, the natural-language planting entry feature allows farmers to describe activities in everyday language, which the AI converts into structured records for confirmation.

Several factors were considered during the development of GeoFarmer. Farmer usability was prioritised through a mobile-first interface, plain language, large touch targets, a chat assistant and natural-language data entry. Agronomic considerations included crop families, nitrogen fixation, nutrient demand, crop duration, slope, erosion risks and the relationship between soil texture and crop water requirements.

Data integrity was another major consideration. Missing values are not estimated, and the sources, spatial resolutions and measurement units of datasets are tracked. Simulated demonstration records are also distinguished from actual observations. To promote trust, every suitability score and recommendation includes an explanation, and the application avoids guaranteeing crop yields or financial returns.

AI safety was addressed through fact-based prompts, automatic verification, a retry mechanism and a rules-based fallback. Privacy was considered by using demonstration farmer identities rather than real personal information. The project also prioritises affordability and accessibility through free and open-source technologies, cached AI responses and compatibility with ordinary smartphone browsers. Scalability was considered by designing a data pipeline that allows additional NASA and soil datasets to be incorporated without requiring major changes to the application. Finally, agricultural expertise remains important, with scoring thresholds identified for review by agronomists and final decisions left to farmers and extension officers.

Despite its capabilities, GeoFarmer currently has some limitations. Although the application evaluates crop suitability using six environmental factors, only two factors, slope and sand content, currently contribute to the available crop scores. Temperature, rainfall, soil pH, nitrogen and other required datasets are either unavailable or not yet fully integrated into the scoring process. The application communicates these limitations rather than presenting incomplete assessments as fully validated recommendations.

Additionally, the farm parcels and farmer records currently represent simulated demonstration data rather than verified operational farm records. Rainfall, temperature and NDVI datasets have not yet been integrated. Soil pH, organic carbon and nitrogen are currently represented as relative levels rather than direct field measurements.

The next phase of development will focus on integrating NASA rainfall and temperature datasets to enable all six suitability factors to contribute to crop assessments. Additional water-stress maps will also be developed to help farmers understand the relationship between environmental conditions and crop water requirements. The team also intends to introduce a comparison feature that will allow farmers to evaluate at least three crop rotation strategies side by side, including their existing rotation practices. These comparisons will present supporting evidence, potential benefits, information gaps and associated risks.

Further improvements will allow farmers to customise their agricultural priorities, such as conserving water, improving soil health, reducing erosion or maximising income. The project will also incorporate measured soil values where available and involve agronomists in reviewing and validating the crop suitability thresholds.

Ultimately, GeoFarmer demonstrates how geospatial technologies, NASA Earth observation data, machine learning and artificial intelligence can be combined to address practical agricultural challenges. By transforming complex environmental datasets into understandable, transparent and locally relevant recommendations, the project seeks to strengthen smallholder farming decisions, promote sustainable soil management and support climate-resilient agriculture in Ejura-Sekyedumase Municipality and beyond.
